speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST BERTRAND (Acting Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO SUPPLIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I make a very quiet statement with respect to supplies of feed grain in British Columbia.
In answer to various inquiries and representations which have been made in the house in respect to a present shortage of supplies

of feed grain in British Columbia, I wish to state that the present situation is acute in eastern Canada as well as in British Columbia. It has not been possible for western shippers to satisfy the effective over-all demand, which has been augmented by the concern over eastern crops.
During recent weeks the bulk of the movement in coarse grains for feed has been to eastern Canada, with comparatively little moving to British Columbia. Oats and barley shipped to eastern Canada are sold on the basis of ceiling prices in store Fort William/ Port Arthur, 65 cents for oats, plus charges for shipment and handling east of Fort William/Port Arthur, less freight subsidy paid by the government. The same grains shipped to British Columbia are sold on the basis of ceiling prices in store Vancouver, plus handling charges, less freight subsidy paid by government. The current over-all shortage of coarse grains as compared with effective demand has resulted in the purchase of these grains by western interior mills, or for shipment to eastern Canada, on the basis of Vancouver export freight rates whereas previously coarse grains were purchased in Alberta on the basis of Fort William/Port Arthur freight rates and were shipped to British Columbia to the full extent of the requirements of that province at approximately two to three cents per bushel less than would have been the case had they been purchased on the Vancouver rate. In other words, British Columbia requirements were filled first and the balance of the oats and barley then moved eastward.
In, view of the changed circumstances, it may probably be necessary for the British Columbia feeder to pay from two to three cents per bushel more for his feed oats and barley than has formerly been the case; that is. he will pay $1.90 a hundredweight for feed oats. But even though he does pay such increased prices, they are still within the ceiling price regulations currently in effect and will still be lower than those now paid by the eastern consumer.
The government no longer possesses the power to direct shipments of oats and barley from Alberta into British Columbia, but it is felt that the British Columbia dealers can place themselves in a competitive position with respect to the eastern trade and will thus have equal access to available supplies. The situation is under constant review by the Department of Agriculture and the Canadian wheat board. It is felt that the companies who have traditionally serviced the British Columbia market will continue to

United Nations
supply these requirements on a basis of equality, having regard to available supplies.
I should add that with respect to feed wheat, the British Columbia market is currently amply supplied. During the last two weeks, approximately 400,000 bushels of low-grade wheat for feeding purposes has been released by the Canadian wheat board to the trade at Vancouver, and further reserves are being held at Alberta country points for shipment to British Columbia in accordance with indicated requirements.
It is reasonable to assume that if western crop conditions continue as favourable as they are at present, producers' marketings will increase, thus relieving the present tight situation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to answer a question asked yesterday by the
hon. member for Brant (Mr. Charlton) in respect to the advertising of Canadian cheese in Great Britain.
During the war and since, the sale in the United Kingdom of cheese and other strictly rationed products as national products has not been permitted. Advertising generally has not been considered desirable and certain types of advertising have been prohibited. The dominions, including Canada, accordingly discontinued all advertising. Recently some general forms of advertising have been undertaken, and in this regard Canada has required by regulation that all Canadian cheese exported be marked "Canada". Every Canadian cheddar cheese weighing more than sixty pounds now exported bears the word "Canada" fifty-eight times.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER- CANADIAN DELEGATION TO FIFTH SESSION OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER- CANADIAN DELEGATION TO FIFTH SESSION OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will be aware that this day marks an important anniversary. On June 26, 1945, at the city of San Francisco, the charter of the united nations was signed in the name of the peoples of fifty nations. These nations, which had fought together successfully in war, now resolved to combine their efforts to accomplish the noble aims which they had written into the charter.
The organization which they thus created was to have within its purview every aspect of international action. In the important field of international economic and social cooperation Canada has had a particular interest. Export trade is the basis of this country's employment and prosperity, and Canada has therefore a real stake in the economic well-being of the world. It is in our own interest for us to do all we can to assist in its restoration and maintenance. Economic isolation is for Canada, as for all nations, as impractical a policy as political isolation.
The importance of this aspect of the work of the united nations is recognized in the preamble of the charter in the resolution "to employ international machinery for the promotion of economic and social advancement of all peoples" and thus "to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom." For the achievement of these ends the economic and social council was created. It was given responsibility, under the author-
Wheat

ity of the general assembly, for the solution of international economic, social, health and related problems.
In the discharge of this extensive task the economic and social council supervises and controls the subordinate machinery of commissions and subcommissions and coordinates the activities of the various specialized agencies with which it has entered into relationship. This important work is less spectacular and less well known than that of other united nations organs. It is, however, the real foundation of international cooperation and of lasting peace.
The united nations and its organs have given us the opportunity of cooperating to rebuild a world economic system. It is too easy, in the midst of the difficulties and risks involved in this great task, to surrender to impatience and dissatisfaction with the measure of progress which has been made in these two short years. We must, however, Temember that the aims of the charter cannot be lightly won. Every effort is required to make the work of the economic and social council a success and Canada has, I think, a particular contribution to make.
I am particularly pleased to announce on this day the Canadian delegation which will attend the fifth session of the economic and social council, scheduled to commence in New York on July 19. My colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), will head the delegation. Doctor George F. Davidson, the deputy minister of welfare, will be the minister's alternate, and officers of the departments of External Affairs and of National Health and Welfare will serve as advisers. I am sure hon. members will join with me in wishing our delegation every success in its endeavour.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER- CANADIAN DELEGATION TO FIFTH SESSION OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am very glad the Prime Minister has brought this before the house. I have always felt that despite the difficulties that confront the nations which form the united nations, they should not deter us. When we think that we have been a confederation for eighty years and yet have not achieved complete unity throughout the country, we should not be alarmed at the difficulties which have arisen in connection with the united nations.
I am glad the Prime Minister emphasized the work of the specialized agencies of the economic and social council; for I believe, in spite of the fact that the glare of public opinion is on the security council, the greatest hope for world peace lies in laying the foundation of an economic and social order which will bring justice to all peoples.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF 1SM7-48 PROGRAMME FOR ONTARIO WINTER WHEAT
speechtext:
On behalf of my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) who is primarily responsible in the matter of wheat marketing, and in my own capacity as the minister responsible for price control, I wish to advise the house of the government's 1947-48 programme for Ontario winter wheat.
In announcing the 1946-47 policy last July, it was pointed out that the government at that time had in mind an increase in the ceiling price applicable to Ontario wheat, but that, owing to developments in price control last summer, it was necessary to continue the ceiling at $1.26 for the crop year ending June 30, 1947. The position of the Ontario wheat producer, however, was improved by the inclusion of a subsidy of nine cents per bushel and a payment of five cents per bushel at the time of delivery, as a fixed and final payment from the Ontario wheat flour equalization fund. For 1946-47 the Ontario wheat producer, therefore, received the ceiling price of $126 per bushel, Montreal basis, plus an additional 14 cents per bushel, bringing the total price up to $1.40 per bushel.
For the crop year beginning July 1, 1947, the government has decided to increase the ceiling price of Ontario wheat to $1.55 per bushel, Montreal basis, bringing it approximately into line with the domestic price at which the wheat board sells western hard wheat. Appropriate adjustments will be made in ceiling prices applicable to products of Ontario winter wheat. With this increase in the ceiling price, a direct subsidy will not be required during the coming year.
In addition to the increased price authorized by the new ceiling of $1.55 per bushel Montreal basis, producers will receive at time of delivery a payment in respect to equalization fees collected on exports of Ontario winter wheat flour. This payment will be eight cents per bushel. The amount of equalization fees collected by the government will vary depending on the difference between $1.55 and prices on world markets, but it is considered desirable, in order to reduce administrative costs and to give a measure of certainty to producers, to fix the producers' payment at a definite figure, representing the estimated total receipts during the year.
In accordance with government policy, steps will be taken to prevent fortuitous profits in respect of stocks of Ontario winter wheat and flour on June 30.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This bill contains a number of amendments to the criminal code. There are thirty-four sections in it, and it would be difficult to explain the bill on the first reading, since it deals with so many subjects. The various provisions of the bill will speak for themselves. I might mention one important section. It is proposed to add a new part to the criminal code, called part X (A), dealing with habitual criminals. This part has been recommended by the commissioners on uniformity of legislation, and in the main follows United Kingdom legislation on the same subject. The new part will provide for the preventive detention for an indeterminate period of those who, over eighteen years of age, are convicted four times of indictable offences, the first three of which are punishable with at least five years' imprisonment, and who are leading persistently criminal lives.
The preventive detention will not be automatic but will be discretionary with the court. No person will be tried on a charge of being 83166-299
an habitual criminal unless the attorney general of the province in which the accused is to be tried consents. Provision is made for periodic review by the Minister of Justice of the condition, history and circumstances of the person preventively detained, with a view to determining whether he will be placed out on licence, and if so, on what conditions.
While legislation of this kind was recommended by the Archambault commission, the government has no wish to be dogmatic about the necessity for it, and while recommending it, is prepared to give careful consideration to any views which may be expressed by members of the house regarding it.
There are a number of other important provisions but I think they could be explained more properly when I move the second reading of the bill.

subsubtopic: RUSSIAN WIFE OF CANADIAN CITIZEN-MRS. GEORGE F. POWER-QUESTION OF EXIT VISA
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Further to a question raised recently in the house by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), can the minister say if there is now any indication whether the Soviet authorities will without further delay grant Mrs. George Power an exit visa permitting her to be reunited with her husband in Canada?
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): The only answer I can give to the hon. member's question is to make to the house a statement of the facts about this matter as they appear to be up to this time. These are the facts.
Mr. George F. Power of the Department of External Affairs was posted to the Canadian embassy in the U.S.S.R. in April, 1943. While in Moscow he met and married Miss Eleanora V. Kuznetsova, a ballerina. His wife is a Soviet citizen. She is also, because of her marriage, a British subject. The marriage was performed by civil contract on February 4, 1945, and was solemnized in a Roman Catholic church a few days later.
Mr. Power left Moscow on July 6, 1945, to return to the Department of External Affairs. Thus Mr. and Mrs. Power lived together for only five months before his return to duty in Ottawa. It was their confident hope at the time that she would join him in this country at an early date. However, nearly two years after Mr. Power's departure, they are still separated for reasons beyond their control.
Mrs. Power applied for a Soviet exit visa in February, 1945, shortly after her marriage. This application was refused in July, 1945. Since then the Canadian embassy in Moscow has approached the Soviet government six times on behalf of Mrs. Power in an effort to secure permission for her to leave the U.S.S.R. However, Mrs. Power has not yet been able to secure an exit visa and no reason has been given by the Soviet authorities for withholding permission for her to rejoin her husband.
The first approach by the Canadian embassy to the Soviet government was made in September, 1945, when Mr. Wilgress, who was then Canadian ambassador in Moscow, discussed the matter orally with Mr. Vyshinsky, Vice-Minister of Foreign Affairs in the U.S.S.R. Mr. Vyshinsky, in explaining the reasons for the delay, said that it was necessary for the Soviet authorities to make a thorough investi-

Inquiries oj the Ministry
gation into each application for an exit visa in order to be sure of the bona fides of the marriage before the visa could be granted to the Soviet wife of a foreigner. He added that each such investigation required some time. In March, 1946, Mr. Wilgress wrote to Mr. Vyshinsky. He pointed out that a year had elapsed) since Mrs. Power had first made her application for an exit visa and that the investigation must surely have been completed. He requested that the visa be granted without further delay. Two further approaches to the Soviet Ministry of Foreign Affairs were made by the Canadian embassy in 1946, one in July and one in November. These all resulted in the same reply-that a decision by the competent Soviet authorities had not yet been made.
On March 20, 1947, Mr. Wilgress wrote to Mr. Molotov, the Minister for Foreign Affairs. Mr. Wilgress stated that, as he was sincerely desirous that relations between Canada and the U.S.S.R. should be placed on the friendliest possible basis, he trusted that it might now be possible for the Soviet authorities to grant an exit visa to Mrs. Power.
On April 5, 1947, Mr. Wilgress, in a personal conversation with Mr. Molotov, referred to his letter of March 20 and expressed the hope that a favourable decision could bo reached before he left Moscow to take up his new post as minister to Switzerland.
In the past, permission has been given on a number of occasions to Soviet women married to British subjects to join their husbands. It is true that by a decree of the praesidium of the Supreme Soviet of the U.S.S.R. of February 15, 1947. marriages between citizens of the U.S.S.R. and foreigners were prohibited. But this cannot affect Mrs. Power's status, as at the time of the marriage in February, 1945, Soviet women were free to marry foreigners.
The Canadian government therefore considers the continued postponement of the grant of an exit visa to Mrs. Power an incomprehensible action on the part of a friendly state. There is no doubt that the marriage was entered into in good faith by both parties, that there is mutual affection, that Mr. Power is able to take good care of his wife, and that if Mre. Power were permitted to come to Canada she would, as a Canadian citizen, reflect credit both on the country of her adoption and the country of her birth. Mrs. Power's application for a Soviet exit visa is the only outstanding application for the wife of a Canadian. The Canadian government sincerely trusts that, in the interests of friendly relations between our two countries, the Soviet authorities will, without further 83166-299*
delay, grant Mrs. Power an exit visa permitting her to be reunited with her husband in Canada.

speechtext:
Nearly a week ago I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to the situation which is developing in the marketing of Canadian apples. The question was raised again two days ago. The minister indicated that he was not sure whether it fell within the jurisdiction of his department, and I understood that he undertook to bring it to the attention of his colleagues and that he would make a [DOT] statement. May I ask today that the Prime Minister give consideration to that matter. It is simply this. A statement has been issued that the British government will not this year be buying Canadian apples as in the past, and it leaves a serious situation facing the fruit growers. My question was: Has the government considered the matter yet, and has it any statement to make with regard to that problem?

make at the moment, but I hope to have some minister reply to my hon. friend in the course of the next week.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
I should like to refer to paragraph (b) of this section in so far as it amends section 3, subsection 1 of the act. I should like to say a word or two to the minister and invite his comments. It is a little difficult to discuss a section like this when one does not agree with the basic position taken. When I say that, I have in mind the difference -of opinion between us. The minister feels that old age pensions should be a joint dominion-provincial responsibility, and I feel that it should be a one hundred per cent federal responsibility. In that connection I support the position taken by the Prime Minister in 1931, particularly on June 2. However, the minister has taken his stand on that and that seems to be the government's position so I shall not argue it. I want to speak, so far as I can, within the terms that are set forth here.
This clause (b) gives to the provinces the right to specify two things: first, the maximum pension and, second, the amount of other income to be allowed to the pensioner up to a maximum. Of course in both cases there is a ceiling created by the effect of section 8 of S50 a month to the single old age pensioner. My quarrel with this section, looking at it on the government's own terms, is, first, that it does not specify a minimum pension, and, second, that the $50 ceiling has the effect of a specific maximum. It seems to me that that is laying a basis for varying pensions, both as to the amount and as to the extent of the means test, across the country. It does seem to me that if the government is going to do it through a joint dominion-provincial responsibility, an effort should be made to achieve some uniformity in the plan. I feel that this section should contain a minimum for the pension, which it does not, and that it should be possible for a province which wants to raise the pension to as high as $40 or S50 a month to lead up to that by permitting other allowable income.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The fact of the matter is that in this parliament we represent Canadians from all the nine provinces and it is our duty to try to protect the rights of Canadian citizens everywhere. I know the minister keeps talking about provincial responsibility in connection with this matter as though it were a social service question, but I see it rather as a matter of right. It will be remembered that the essence of those proposals was that the dominion would assume one hundred per cent responsibility for the payment of a pension without a means test to every person in Canada seventy years of age and over. There were no strings attached; there was no means test, there was no limitation. The dominion was to assume full responsibility and there were no restrictions. parliament, and a responsibility which this government proclaimed to all Canada two years ago and since that it was prepared to assume. Now we have a complete reversal of that position and we see the dominion entering into agreements with the provinces and tying the hands of the provinces, so that if the provinces want to make changes they have to enter into new agreements with the dominion government within the scope of the pension of S30 a month to which the dominion contributes 75 per cent.
Under paragraph (b) of this section provision is made for inserting in the agreement stipulations in regard to the total of income which may be received by a pensioner. That raises directly the point which I sought to make the other day, and it is this. That strict limitation imposed by the dominion in this act and in the agreements which will be made under it as to the total which a pensioner may receive by way of allowable income is a brake placed by the dominion upon the provinces in the matter of making contributions. It is idle for the minister to say that the provinces can pay as much as they like. That is not so, because if the pensioner has any earned income at all, and if the combined total of dominion pension of $30 and the provincial supplement and the earned income amounts to over $600 a year, where does the reduction take place? Not in the provincial supplement. It comes off the $30 a month to which the dominion is contributing. Therefore you are going to discourage the pensioner from earning income and the province from contributing. It is of no use for the minister to shake his head. He has been shaking his head and wagging his tongue and interrupting everybody throughout this debate, and members have learned by this time to pay little or no attention to what he says. What I am saying, without the slightest fear of contradiction from the minister or from anybody to your right, Mr. Chairman, is that this set-up discourages any pensioner from seeking to earn income on his own behalf, and it discourages the province from contributing supplements, because if the effect of the two combined, together with the pension of $30, is to give the pensioner a total income of over $600 a year, the reduction does not come off the provincial supplement but off the pension to which the dominion is contributing. What encouragement is there in that for the provinces to try to eke out an insufficient pension by granting a supplement? Here is the minister throwing responsibility on the provinces and trying to make a good fellow of himself by raising the total of pension and raising the total of allowable income. But the further you look into it 83166-300
the more hollow' the whole scheme appears, the bigger the sham it is shown to be. For the minister to picture this as a measure of social reform just shows how far he has failed to appreciate even the elementary significance of social reform.

I wish to refer to paragraph (b) of subsection 1 of section 3. The paragraph reads:

'Subject to sections eight and eight A of this act, in every agreement made pursuant to this subsection the province shall specify the maximum pension to be paid by the province and shall provide for the reduction of such maximum pension by the amount of any income received by a pensioner in excess of an amount of income to be specified in such agreement.
I fear, Mr. Chairman, that we are going to run into the same difficulty when this act comes into operation as we had a few years ago when several provinces endeavoured to raise the pension which was then stipulated at $20 a month. It will be recalled that some of the provinces at that time were desirous of increasing the pension from $20 to $25. A discussion arose between the provinces and the federal government as to whether or not these provinces would be permitted to increase the pension under the regulations laid down by the federal government. Some provinces did increase the pension regardless of that, and a battle ensued on whether these pensions would be reduced by the federal government. The federal government did accede to the desire and allowed the pension to go up to $25 a month. That was not done according to the regulations but by agreement with the federal government, and the provinces did increase their pension. Immediately some of the provinces raised the amount of pension to $30 because they realized that with the increased cost of living the pensioners could not exist on the amount of pension then paid; but again they were subject to the regulations and the pensioner was put in the position where at least the share of his pension which was being paid by the federal government would be reduced according to the amount that it was increased by the province.
Today we have the situation that a province may set the maximum pension paid; so long as that maximum is less than the $30 a month the federal government will pay seventy-five per cent of it. But the moment that the provinces desire to go above the total income of $50, including the pension and the earned income, the federal government will again cut their share of the contribution by the amount that the total exceeds the pension plus the income. That will put the pensioners in exactly the position that they were in years ago. In fact it prohibits any province from giving more than $50 a month. When I say $50 a month I mean $30 contributed by the province and the federal government plus the income which the pensioner is allowed, which makes a total of $50 a month. The moment that a province desires to give the pensioner another $5 the federal government can apply the regulations again and their share of the

Old Age Pensions
seventy-five per cent of the $30 will be reduced accordingly. If, a province recognizes the fact that because of the increased cost of living, which, is soaring day after day, an old age pensioner cannot have a decent standard of living on the amount alloted, and if it desires to raise that amount, then the federal government can invoke a section of the act-not a regulation, because it will now be in the act- and reduce the amount of their contribution to the province. We should try to get away from the situation which faced the provinces a few years ago under the old regulations. I suggest to the minister that they permit the province at least-because it will not cost the federal government any more; it will be nothing out of the federal government's pocket -to pay as large a pension as they desire without the federal government reducing its seventy-five per cent of the $30. That would not be asking the federal government to do anything; it would not be losing anything, but the provinces could increase the pension to the amount they desired.

But I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to follow me as I draw your attention to citations in Beauchesne, third edition. I firmly believe that because of the wording of the resolution which preceded the bill, this committee is in the unusual position of having the right to increase the amount of money provided in this section.
The usual procedure with respect to a resolution preceding a bill is that it shall state the maximum amount of money to be provided by the bill. The rules state that care should be taken to see that this is done. As one looks over past history he finds that it has been done in the vast majority of cases. In fact I cannot find an instance in which it has not been done, except this particular one. For example, when old age pensions were first introduced in 1926 by Hon. J. H. King, who was then acting minister of labour, the
Old Age Pensions

resolution preceding the bill, as found in Hansard for March 26, 1926, at page 1937, gave the full details of the old age pension plan and stipulated the maximum amount. Similarly, when family allowances were introduced in this house on June 22, 1944, the resolution preceding the bill, to be found at page 4052 of Hansard of that year, gave all the details, including the maximum amounts to be paid to children of various ages. The same is true of the War Service Grants Act of 1944. The same is true of other money bills which we have had before us this session In all cases except this one, the resolution preceding the bill stipulated the maximum amount of money which was to be provided under that bill. But in this case the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he introduced the resolution which was passed on June 17, as recorded at page 4233 of Hansard, worded that resolution as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Pensions Act which will enlarge the scope of the act by providing increases in the pension payable and the income allowable to pensioners and by modifying certain of the eligibility requirements for pension.
Using language which you will recognize in Beauchesne in a moment, I draw your attention, sir, to the fact that that resolution was framed in general terms and1 did not specify a maximum amount. If you, Mr. Chairman, and hon. members will turn to Beauchesne, third edition, pages 168 and 169, you will find citation 439. I will not read the whole of it because the first part is introductory. The last two sentences are the ones which count. The second last sentence is the one with which we are all familiar. It reads:
The constitutional principle which vests in the crown the sole responsibility of incurring national expenditure forbids an increase by the Commons of a sum demanded on behalf of the crown for the service of the state.

This principle, however, is apparently disregarded when the recommendation of the crown is given to a resolution empowering the expenditure of public money which, framed in general terms, places no limitation on the amount of expenditure to be authorized by the resolution.
That is what we have in this case.

minister was why, in this measure, the dominion government is not assuming the whole cost of old age pensions for. people over seventy. I asked that question because this government two years ago undertook to do it in agreement with the provinces. Hon. members have 'heard the minister's answers and the public will be prepared to assess those answers on their merits. What has he said? He said that we have not a dominion provincial agreement with all the provinces. He has said that the provinces are not paying enough, and he declares he is on firm ground with his present proposal, which, in his own words, will be an added contribution by the dominion of some $20 million. In his own statement just now he admitted that the cost of old age pensions at seventy without the means test would be $200 million. That was the proposal made by this government two years ago, and the committee has heard the minister's answer as to why they discarded it. I suggest that is not the real answer at all.
I am going to read now the views of a man who is supposed to be an authority on this matter. He was quoted by the minister himself as an authority on social questions and as being probably more interested than any other human being in this house in this matter. I am referring to a man who made a speech in this chamber sixteen years ago on this question. I refer to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). This is what he had to say on the question of the share of cost that should be borne by the dominion government. And this statement was made before they ever had a thought of dominion-provincial agreements. I quote from the House of Commons Debates, 1931, June 2, at page 2260, the words of the present Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Yesterday the minister
called that a discarded opinion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
This is what the right
hon. gentleman said:
It was recognized that an amendment to the British North America Act would take some time, and for that reason the government of the day-
He was speaking of the Liberal government.
-adopted the method of agreeing to give these grants in aid to the provinces on condition that they would carry out a scheme framed by the federal government which would be similar in all the provinces. .
An hon. Member: A vicious principle.
Mr. Mackenzie King: The principle, from a financial point of view was unsound. I am quite prepared to concede that. But I will go a step further and say that, in my opinion, this parliament ought to remedy the unsoundness of the
Old Age Pensions

principle, not by discontinuing to vote money lor old age pensions, but by assuming the entire obligation, one hundred per cent. This government should take over the whole scheme and itself pay out the money. That is the position that should be taken; that is the proper way to remedy what there is of unsoundness in the principle.
Mr. Chaplin: That is an extension of the vicious principle.
Mr. Mackenzie King: No; on the contrary, it is getting rid of what is vicious. I wish my hon. friend to follow me in this. The principle of old age pensions is a thoroughly sound one.
I drop a couple of lines.
Obviously the principle is thoroughly sound. I have always taken that position and have fought strenuously for it; and to get that principle recognized by parliament I was prepared to go so far as to support a grant in aid, which I am perfectly frank to admit was, from the point of view of financing, an unsound method. Now I say, let_ us recognize that the principle of old age pensions itself is perfectly sound and involves an obligation which the federal parliament should assume. Let us undertake to administer the Old Age Pensions Act from Ottawa and have all the moneys which are necessary for the payment of those pensions voted by this parliament.
That is the view of a man who is quoted by the minister of health as an authority. Yet, in the face of that and in the face of the position of the government and their offer to pay 100 per cent of it two years ago, they come forward with this seventy-five per cent proposal. In the face of a plan which the Prime Minister was advocating and which would cost this country $200 million, the minister brings forward this plan of giving only $60 a year of an increase to old age pensioners.
I now wish to ask the minister another question. In the face of the decision of the government to eliminate the means test, why does he come forward now with a plan which perpetuates it? In their offer two years ago they knew the cost of that plan. I ask the minister to answer now why he comes forward with an entirely different plan.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

May I point out to the hon. gentleman that I respect the high constitutional authority to which he has just made reference.
Mr. MaeINNIS: He was in opposition at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I would remind the gentleman that there are extenuating circumstances which perhaps will explain the situation, and these I give. But before doing that, may I remind the hon. member that, before the federal election in 1930, the then leader of the opposition, Lord Bennett, said that if he got into office he would propose the taking over by the federal government of the full

cost of old age pensions. That was also the attitude taken by the followers of my hon. friend under other leadership all through the parliaments between 1926 and 1930. When Lord Bennett became Prime Minister of Canada in 1930, he did make a change in the Old Age Pensions Act by increasing the federal contribution from fifty per cent, at which figure it then was, to seventy-five per cent. He did not do what he said he would do, namely, bring the contribution up to 100 per cent. That is an important point to note. Since the Prime Minister made that statement, if my hon. friend will read the debate, as I am sure he has done, he will find that the whole context of it reveals an attitude which was shared not only by the leader of this party, but by the house in general; but the statement was in respect only of a scheme for old age pensions. The proposals which were laid before the provinces in 1945 went away beyond that, They involved considerations which, I would again remind the hon. gentleman, called for the expenditure of over $600,000,000 annually, to be paid by the federal and provincial governments. I think one must read the statement made by the Prime Minister, which my hon. friend has so correctly quoted, in the light of those proposals. I now come to the question about the means test. I tried to indicate yesterday that no country in the world has eliminated the means test, even those which have a contributory system. New Zealand has a contributory system, and she has a universal free system. Australia has both systems. So has Great Britain, and so has' the United States. In all those cases they retained the means test. No country where there is a universal free system has abandoned the means test.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Would the minister allow me to make a point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. MaeINNIS: In New Zealand the universal superannuation does not carry a means test, It has not reached its full amount, but it will not carry a means test even when it reaches the full amount.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

Old Age Pensions

As I say, the proposals must be taken as a plan which will cost this country a great deal of money every year, and we shall be committed to it for the rest of our lives. I am not opposed to that, but I am pointing out what it means. When the government had those discussions with the provinces we did not say we would do this or would do that. We said we were prepared to do all of these things, but they are all integrated. That must be kept in mind. I did not want to bring before this house a proposal with respect to this measure-and the elimination of the means test would have meant that very thing-which would give anyone the chance of saying, "You have now done something very generous. That will be your substitute for the proposals themselves." To hon. members who are interested in seeing a social security programme built up
gradually, stage by stage, each government participating, I have no hesitation in saying that I am sure, on fair reflection, they will see the wisdom of the statement I have just made. We have not taken away the means test as applied to people of seventy and over, for the reason I have mentioned. What we have done is to liberalize the means test to a considerable extent.

I do not say this does everything; I do not offer it as a full and final measure, but I suggest with great sincerity that these figures, in the light of our obligations, which are tremendous; in the light of our proposals to the provinces; in view of the fact that these are among the most liberal means test provisions to be found anywhere in the world, do not offer justification for much of the criticism which has been made. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The question I asked the minister was why he has come forward now with a proposal which does not eliminate the means test, after the government undertook in their plans two years ago to eliminate it. One part of the minister's answer is that no country in the world has eliminated the means test. But the government knew that fact when it proposed to eliminate the means test two years ago. The minister now pleads the huge cost of these social services as an excuse for not proceeding with the government's original plans. He said the great plans they had in connection with all these things would cost the dominion and the provinces $600 million", and therefore the government could not proceed with them except to the extent of about $20 million. I want to ask the minister this. They did bring in a social security plan-family allowances-which cost this country $250 million a year, about five times the cost of old age pensions, and they did not require any means test- for it. I ask why they did not have a means test in that case, and why they persist in retaining the means test under the old age pension scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I want to say to the hon. gentleman again, as I have said twice already today, perhaps inadequately, and as I have said before in the debate, that the proposal to the provinces regarding the means test was part of a plan. It was conditional. We could not do it by ourselves, in all responsibility, but we were prepared to do it as part of a plan if we were able to get fiscal agreement with the provinces. What my hon. friend is saying is that if you make an agreement to pay a man $1,000 for a horse and he does not give you the horse, you must still give him the $1,000. Really that is the same thing.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

speechtext: My hon. friend made what, I think, was a fair observation, though I do not believe it is valid. He said, "But you did that with regard to family allowances, which cost $250 million. You did not consult the provinces, and you do not have a means test." I wonder if my hon. friend has thought carefully about that observation. That was a matter of financial assistance to children who were supposed to be at school, not earning money. How could you apply a means test to them?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I have two or three other questions to ask the minister. I think he let the cat out of the bag a minute or two ago in connection with this matter when he spoke of the huge cost of the government's social security and public investment plan, which was to be $600 million. That is why this government have come along with this little plan; they are afraid to face the people with the costly plans they put forward two years ago. That is why this plan is now brought forward. The government can take one side or the other of this position, but not both. It is now trying to make scapegoats of a couple of provinces that did not come in. It says it is their fault that we cannot have this huge social security and public investment plan which cost the country $600 million a year. As I said, the minister has let the cat out of the bag. The government is afraid to face the public with that huge expenditure. That is why these plans are whittled down to what they are today.
I now want to ask the minister another question. Why has the government left entirely out of its proposal the offer of a fifty-fifty plan of public assistance to persons between the age of sixty-five and seventy, the offer it made two years ago? I ask the minister to explain why the government has taken this position, after two short years. I ask him to answer that question in the light of the statements which may be found at page 38 of this so-called green book, containing the 1945 proposals of the government of Canada. This particular feature, deals with the means test and, a little later, with the public assistance proposal for persons under seventy years of age. What did they say about the means test, which the government is now perpetuating? These are their words:
The principal feature of the proposed national old age pensions is the elimination of the means test after reaching age seventy, regarding tnis as unsuitable for the oldest group in the community over eighty per cent of whom are not in fact capable of supporting themselves in useful, re-

Old Age Pensions
munerative work. Payment of pensions as of right to people of this age offers the best kind of economic security.
That is this government, two years ago.
It removes the fear of destitution much more certainly than any other method, and relieves old people of the necessity of seeking work, or of endeavouring to keep on working in unfavourable circumstances and beyond the age at which they should be able to retire, wtihout dependence on charity or burdening the family. In addition to providing a minimum subsistence for those with no other resources, this system would enable other persons with moderate private savings to retire from active work sooner, or in more comfort, than would otherwise be possible.
Then comes this closing sentence:
The removal of the means test would make it possible for these pensions to be administered by the federal government alone on a uniform national basis, without the necessity for provincial participation, and would thereby considerably relieve provincial finances.
That was the view put forward by the government two years ago. But what have we today? A complete denial of that proposal. I ask the minister now why he is doing nothing for people under seventy years of age, in view of what the government had to say two years ago with respect to them.

speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock I was about to refer to the government's promise of two years ago that it would share with the provinces on a fifty-fifty plan for assistance to aged persons between the ages of sixty-five and seventy years. My question is: Why is the government not making any provision to meet that situation now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I thought I had answered that earlier. I can only say that that was part of a full plan which embraced proposals with regard to health, public investment and social security. Each part has to be taken in conjunction with the whole. I was not going to
propose to this parliament at this stage anything which I felt and which the government feels would be regarded as a substitute for a much more all-embracing system of social security, health and public investment.
There is one additional fact with regard to the 65-69 proposal. In that case the responsibility of the provinces would be greater than under the present bill. They were to share the cost of old age assistance to persons between sixty-five and sixty-nine years of age on a fifty-fifty basis, and I may tell my hon. friend that they would not have gone for that proposal.
One must bear in mind that we have made great progress since last year when my predecessor stood in this place when this matter was discussed on the estimates. He was not in the fortunate position I am in today in being able to say that we have agreements on fiscal matters with seven provinces. That means that we have gone a great bit forward since that time and we are much closer to the stage when we shall have a social security conference. I have no doubt in my mind that we shall receive sufficient acceptance by the provinces other than those seven to enable us to deal with the definite proposals we have in mind.
The provinces which are out represent, I will not say all the wealth of the country, but I think it can be stated definitely that they do represent about eighty per cent. Their population is quite large, and two-thirds of the population which would be affected by social security measures are in those two provinces. How long we shall have to wait is another matter. But that is what the hon. gentleman should keep in mind; it is what I have to keep in mind and what the government has had to keep in mind.
We had made broad proposals in the three fields of health, social security and public investment. When one looks at what we were prepared to do in the field of health alone by way of low interest costs for hospitals, by way of attacking tuberculosis and other diseases, by way of planning grants and so on, he will realize that we have a formidable programme, a programme which, I think, we should all aspire to, regardless of our political affiliations.
Those are the objectives which we had in our minds. It was because of those objectives that it is more desirable to have a broad social security scheme than to have one that is lopsided, one that gives relief to only one group. Surely what we should aim at is to give social security assistance to all groups, and that is what the proposals envisage. If w:e do anything that will prejudice
Old Age Pensions

that or give anyone justification for saying that this is a substitute, I believe we would not be doing justice to the Canadian people. I am sure that, on reflection and analysis by those in this house who have given this matter their careful attention and by the public generally in Canada, there will be agreement with the position I am taking.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I have one further
question to ask and a brief statement to make, and then I think I shall have finished. I asked the minister why the government has brought forward no plan for pensions for persons between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine years. Hon. members of the committee have heard the minister's answer, which is again to the effect that he has no over-all agreement with all the provinces. I suggest that that is a very weak answer. The simple fact is that because two of the provinces are not in this agreement today this government is spending S100 million less than it would otherwise have had to raise and spend. The contributions to those provinces would have been something over $100 million. The government does not have to raise that amount under its present plans.
The minister states that to provide old age assistance for persons between the ages of sixty-five and seventy years would cost at least $34,000,000 a year. Let me point out that, because those other two provinces, Ontario and Quebec, are not in this, the government does not have to impose taxes of $100 million; it does not have to pay them that $100 million; and therefore it is more able to finance some of these services than it would if those two provinces were in.
The committee has heard the minister's answer to my question. In the light of that answer, I want to read the views of the government two years ago with respect to assistance to persons of the ages of sixty-five to seventy years as contained in a thoughtful document, namely the proposals of the government in 1945. I read from page 38, as follows:
The minimum age for national old age pensions must be definite and fixed; it cannot vary with individual cases. It must be recognized, however, that there will be an intermediate age group in which a significant minority of persons will be unable, by reason of age, to support themselves without assistance.
This is the government of Canada speaking two years ago.
These persons who, in fact, suffer from the disability which old age pensions are intended to assist, should not be left with no other resources than local poor relief for the temporary period which must elapse till they reach the qualifying age for old age pensions. Accordingly, it is proposed that the existing system of joint dominion-provincial old age assistance on a means-test basis, which it is proposed to

supersede as regards persons of 70 and over, should be adapted to meet the needs in particular eases of persons of age 65-69, with a federal government contribution of 50 per cent of the cost.
And two or three sentences below:
The federal government offers to provide financial assistance and give tangible expression to the national interest in the matter, by contributing 50 per cent of the cost.
I present that considered statement by this government as given two years ago and put it side by side with the statement which the minister made, today in justifying the present measure.

We recommend an amendment to regulation 17 governing the computing of income so as to provide that medical, hospitalization and other extraordinary expenses paid by members of the family as contribution to pensioner or paid out of pensioner's income should not be taken *as income in computing pensioner's income.

government take immediate steps to try and insure that the above recommendations become effective at the very earliest possible date and that every effort be made and continued by this government to bring the above changes into operation.	'

We should consider the pension when it is the sole income. If you take it on that basis, then the pension payable under this measure is $360, and what we have to ask ourselves before passing this measure is this: There are people in Canada, as is proved by the government's own green book, who have no outside income and whose total income, therefore, under this plan will be the pension-$360. . . . married to and living with a sighted spouse, and the total income of such person and his spouse, inclusive of pension is not more than $1,080 a year . . .

I thought he was wise in permitting an open discussion of the whole matter, because in my opinion, we shall make far better progress on this bill if that is done than if there is an attempt to restrict discussion. This matter of old age pensions is exercising this nation from coast to coast, in every hamlet, on every roadside, in every farm home. We cannot have this matter dealt with lightly.
During the discussion the minister made several references to the government's overall scheme, so I gather that this bill is part of an elaborate scheme on the part of this government for rationing scarcity. Where is that new order we heard so much about in 1941 and 1942? Dear me, anyone with any common sense at all knew the government could get money by taxing the very bread out of the mouths of the people; and that if they destroyed the financial independence of the provinces by taking away their taxation fields they could obtain a sum of money which they could ration out meagrely to certain extranecessitous people. There is nothing new about that. They knew about it back in the days of Greece and Rome, and before that. What we were all looking for was a really new order; but anything the minister has said so far, and what he has given us in this bill, certainly do not encourage much hope for anything resembling a new order. As I said a moment ago, it is merely the rationing or

Old Age Pensions
redistribution of scarcity. It represents a definite admission that it is impossible for the people of this country to have more than just so much, and that so much will depend upon the amount of money they happen to have, with no reference at all to the amount of goods they can produce. I have been astonished at the few times anyone during this debate has said anything about the $12,000 million worth of goods we Canadians can produce.

He must recall those words many times with mortification and shame. When the Prime Minister made those remarks in 1934, and again in August, 1935, when he spoke to the Dominion of Canada over the radio from Ottawa, he certainly gave the Canadian people the idea .that he had something in his mind better than what is suggested and outlined by this bill and its monstrous system of penalizing the Canadian people, robbing them of the things they have and redistributing their scarcity. We have had discussions this afternoon as to how many provinces have come in, as to making them pay their share, as to not being able to do anything until we get them all in and that kind of thing. I think I have said enough along that line. All hon. members who have been thinking along that line will admit that I am speaking for them.
Let us turn to what this bill actually does. It proposes to give our old age pensioners $30 a month. There appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail in April, 1947, an article which has been referred to directly and indirectly several times. It states that $28 weekly in 1939-40 was equal to $53 today. I am not going into the question of whether or not those figures are right because I fancy they are, since the Globe and Mail I believe is rather dependable on a matter of that sort. I should like to point out what that, if it is true, means in regard to this bill.
If $53 today is the equal of $28 in 1939-40, it means that this bill is offering to the senior citizens of Canada who have passed their
seventieth year. $15.80 a month in 1939^0 money. When he looks at the bill from that angle all the enthusiasm must die in even the minister's breast.

Our organization is in full accord with and urges your immediate consideration for the enactment of the following amendments in the o'ld age pension regulations:
1.	Payment of pensions be made at 60 years of age.

I thought it was fitting that we should know what we are doing for the people in Winnipeg when we pass this bill as it stands. There can be no possible excuse. Yet that is exactly the sort of thing we face in this house. I shall say very little more. I have been thinking of a little piece of poetry that I have not been able to get out of my mind all during the days that we have been talking of old age pensions. These lines I think everybody has loved. They are from Browning. They go like this:
Grow old along -with me.
The best is yet to be,
The last of life, for which the first was made.
In the light of what I have read here, in the light of this bill, there is a terrible lot of tragedy and pathos in these lines. For our present elderly people there is no possible chance of having the last of life better than the first. They cannot even maintain that health and vigour which would enable them to go and enjoy life if they had the opportunity. Having said that, I shall desist from further discussion.
I believe that every hon. member who is listening to me-and: they are listening so sympathetically, for which I express the greatest appreciation-feels exactly as I do about this matter. Then why do we not do something about it? We cannot do anything about it by continuing to discuss the matter in terms of the present financial system. The leader of the opposition, when he was questioning the minister a while ago, called him to task because he was not doing what his government promised to do two years ago. During the questioning the leader of the opposition did not tell the committee where he himself could get any more money in order to do the desirable things, if he were in power.
When I was a boy and began talking about the fine things we were going to do my father used to say, "Son, talk is cheap but it takes money to buy whiskey." I would say to the members of the Progressive Conservative party, talk is cheap but it takes money to buy whiskey.

The speech of the hon. member for Lethbridge has given me quite a number of ideas. He said that it takes money to buy whiskey. I have often wondered how the old people get along and can ever get a drink, as a matter of fact, on the amount of money that they receive.
I want to address myself particularly to subparagraph (iii) of paragraph (a) of section 4 of this bill which reads as follows: is not an Indian as defined by the Indian Act.
In other words, I want to speak briefly about the only class of people in this country who are now excluded from receiving old age pensions. These people are, of course, the original inhabitants of the country, the Indians.
Listening to the hon. member for Lethbridge recite his long list of food stuffs of various kinds and following that up with a small piece of poetry, I was reminded of a jingle from Shakespeare's "King Lear" which was constantly repeated by the half-mad beggar Tom. Everyone who has read that drama will remember that Tom went around constantly chanting:
But mice and rats and such small deer
Have been Tom's food for seven long year.
As a matter of fact I think it is practically and actually applicable to a lot of our Indians.
Mr. BLACIvMORE: Hear, hear.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Why these people, of all the people of Canada, should be excluded from the benefits of the Old Age Pensions Act I have never been able to understand.
This afternoon, in replying to the hon. member for Broadview, the minister said that there were great difficulties in applying the Old Age Pensions Act to the Indians, because the provinces administered the act and, of course, they would not make any contributions so far as the Indians were concerned, since the Indians are the sole responsibility of the dominion. I should like to tell the minister that if he disregards any provincial contribution whatever and gives the Indians only the 83166-302
amount of the dominion contribution, namely, $22.50, they would be extraordinarily grateful for it. The present situation in which they find themselves is that they get relief in kind in the form of a certain amount of hard rations, amounting on the average, I believe, to around S5 a month. Why the aged among the Indians should be forced to continue on that scale of relief in their old age, while people who came to this country and, as the changes in the act provide, never became citizens, never learned either of our official languages and so forth, are now eligible for the old age pension, is something I cannot personally understand.
At the beginning of this parliament in 1945, I introduced a resolution into the house calling for the payment of old age pensions to the Indians. Everybody who spoke on that resolution-the debate continued all day- including the Minister of Mines and Resources who closed the debate, expressed himself in favour of paying old age pensions to the Indians, including a large number on the government side of the house. The resolution was talked out.
Following that, the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which is considering the Indian Act at the .present time, passed a resolution requesting that old age pensions be extended to the Indians.

The house accepted the report, and therefore I take it that the house as a whole is in favour of extending old age pensions to these people.
I should like to ask the minister what consideration he and the government have given to this resolution which was adopted by the house. He said that it was merely a request for consideration. I should also like to ask him what consideration has been given to giving the Indians the dominion's share of the contribution, in other words $22.50 a

Old Age Pensions

month, because even that limited amount would go a long way toward settling the problems and the difficulties of the Indians.
I do not think it helps much for the minister to say, as he said this afternoon, that the Indians receive other help and that they are in a special situation and so forth. It is quite true that they are in a special situation, but what is the use of being in a special situation if it only entitles you to be semi-starved to death? You would be much better out of that.
The minister said that any Indian can apply for enfranchisement if he wishes. That is quite correct. He can, but it does not mean that it will be granted. As a matter of fact, before an Indian can be enfranchised he has to show that he is likely to be self-sufficient, so that the old Indians who might wish to be enfranchised in order that they can get the old age pension will not be accepted for enfranchisement. Enfranchisement will not be granted to them because they cannot show that they are likely to be able to support themselves. In view of all these things, I would ask the minister to give any reasons, other than the specious ones which have already been given, as to why these people continue to be excluded alone among all the people in Canada, from the benefits of the Old Age Pensions Act.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
can answer when I get through because I want to speak along the same line. If a private member could move an amendment in the manner I would suggest, I rvould move that line 32 in section 4 be repealed. As the member for Calgary East said, we are excluding from the benefits of this act a group of people who are in far greater need than any other group in Canada. We have heard the hon. member for Lethbridge read lists of foodstuffs that can be bought on the present pension, but these Indians have practically no money. The little bit of relief they do get amounts to about $3 a month, perhaps a little more now. That is however, what it used to be. These people are almost starving slowly to death. I do not see why the minister could not have included them in this bill, for the reason that when the former minister of health and welfare brought in the family allowance the Indians were included and they received the benefits of that allowance- As the hon. member for Calgary East said, we have had a committee set up here, and they have held many meetings and have worked hard and have listened to the stories

of the Indians and the terrible needs of the old people among them. That committee brought in its recommendations and moved unanimously that pensions should be given to the old Indians.
In the other chamber on Wednesday, May 7, the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons submitted its report.
I quote:
The joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons appointed to continue and conclude the examination and consideration of the Indian Act (Chapter 98, R.S.C., 1927), and all such other matters as have been referred to the said committee, beg leave to make their third report, as follows:
Your committee unanimously recommend that the government give immediate consideration to the advisability of granting old age pensions to Canadian Indians.
On Wednesday, May 7, 1947, the same third report was presented to the House of Commons:
Your committee unanimously recommends that the government give immediate consideration to the advisability of granting old age pensions to Canadian Indians.
This was concurred in on the 12th day of May. The minister said that they did give consideration, that the report only asked him to consider. But I think the committee, after listening to the story of these Indians, felt that the government should give the benefit to the older Indians. In the Globe and Mail of June 16, 1947, I find a short article dated Vancouver, June 15, Canadian Press, as follows:
The welfare and training branch of the Department of Indian Affairs will recommend that native Indians receive old age pensions and mothers' allowances, and that welfare officers be appointed for each Indian reserve in Canada, it was said tonight.
George Fellowes. schoolmaster on the Chilliwack reserve, about 50 miles east of here, said he had received that information in a letter from Col. B. F. Neary, head of the welfare and training branch at Ottawa.
I suggest that all the different organizations that are in any way connected with Indians realize the terrible poverty they have to go through, and I believe the government is remiss in its duty when it does not extend the benefit to the Indians. The minister should give a better reason than that which he gave just before the supper hour why the Indians are not included in the act.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I wish to add a thought. Sub-paragraph (iii) of paragraph (a) of subsection (1) states:
is not an Indian as defined by the Indian Act.
Under the Indian Act, all Canadian Indians on reserves are considered wards of the gov-

Old Age Pensions
eminent. The manner in which the governments of Canada have fulfilled their obligations to these wards can be debated later, but studies of the living conditions among these people reveal that a large majority of them are living in a shocking state of want, disease and poverty. I have made a study of conditions among them, and I can say that, especially among the aged Indians, the problem is a severe one. In Norway House I saw an aged blind widow on a reserve who had to go every couple of weeks to an agency to get a small ration of flour and salt, scarcely enough to keep body and soul together. The extension of the benefits of this act to the older Indians would be one of the greatest acts of humanity we could perform at the present time, and I know of no group who are in greater need. I know the officials of the department would welcome this. I believe the Canadian people would support this move if they really knew the conditions among the Indians. It has been proved further that members in every party on both sides of the house would support it.
I think the clause should be deleted for another great reason. It draws one more line between the Canadian people and this group of 130,000 people who are placed on reserves, a minority people who have been segregated on these reserves and relegated to an inferior position. That should not prevail in Canada.
I believe the Canadian people will support the move to raise the Indians to higher standards and give them an opportunity for a fuller life, but this clause widens the gulf and there is plenty of evidence to show that these people do not trust the whites who have placed them in that position. They have reason to distrust the whites on account of their actions in the past, and at this time particularly such a move as has been suggested would be the part of statesmanship toward a people who are potentially great. In Canada we claim that all the people have the rights of the democracy, and it is shameful that these people should be placed in a position where they have very little opportunity for redress, practically no voice, and very little in the way of an appeal against the injustice under which they may suffer or think they suffer.
I plead with the minister to consider carefully the withdrawing of the provision to which I have referred. If he will do that it will form the basis on which these minority people can start to build up their trust, and it will restore faith on the part of these people in Canadians who have relegated them to a position of inferiority.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The point discussed tonight with regard to our Indian population is a problem with which, I am sure, every member in this house will have full sympathy. This bill can only deal with that class of Indians who are within the enfranchised group. A thorough study is being made by the Indian affairs committee, not only with regard to old age pensions for Indians, but equally with regard to the whole problem of the health, welfare and education of Indians. I know the hon. member for Davenport is greatly interested in that subject; he has discussed it with me. The government is looking with great interest to the work of that committee. What it proposes to do with regard to the Indians will be done at the right time in a special measure; and I think the problem should be dealt with as a special problem. We are studying the work of this committee in all its features. When the committee has made its report and when certain other studies which are being made, such as surveys in the field and the like, are completed, we shall be in a position to deal, not only with old age pensions for Indians, but with the broader aspects as well.

what the minister has said. He said when they-and I understood that he meant the government-received the report of this committee which is now considering the Indian Act, they would deal with it. subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The reason I have already given. We wi^h to deal with the Indian problem as a whole. The hon. gentleman is a member of that committee; and, as he knows, the problem is much more than that of old age pensions for the Indians. We intend to deal with the problem as a whole. This bill is merely an arrangement by which we provide assistance for the maintenance of the aged, through grants, as it were, made to the provinces, seventy-five per cent of which cost we assume and they assume twenty-five per cent. The Indian, on the other hand, is our full constitutional responsibility. It is in the light of that that we are following the deliberations of the committee, not only with respect to t'his one matter, but with respect to the whole matter of the health and welfare of Indians.

speechtext:
That was the story that was produced in 1945, when the resolution
Old Age Pensions

to give the Indians the old age pension was introduced. That was the story the government put up then, namely, that the whole Indian question was to be referred to a committee or a royal commission; at that time it had not been decided which it would be. Following the deliberations of that body, their entitlement to the old age pension, along with other matters, was to be settled. That was two years ago. I consider it extremely unlikely that this committee will finish its work, get its report in and have it implemented for another two years. In the meantime the Indians are suffering. I do not think it is good enough for the minister to rise and say, "As soon as we have studied all the broad aspects of this thing, we shall be able to make a decision." The very fact that this committee, which has now spent two years in studying the question, has made an interim report recommending that the old age pension be paid to Indians, should be good enough as far as that particular aspect of the question is concerned. I do not think it is necessary for the government to wait any longer before taking action on that particular phase. This excuse, as I would call it, which the minister has been putting up, namely, that we must wait for the committee to finish its work in order to consider the entire broad question, is an extraordinarily flimsy excuse, and one which he and the government should not for a moment attempt to rely on.
