Before we get too far away from the discussion of the Indians, I should like to say just a word or two on that point. I have had the privilege of being a member of the joint committee on the Indian Act for two years. My interest in the Indians has always been great, but it has been tremendously increased as a result of the work of that committee. I wish to say just a word in support of the proposition that Indians should receive the old age pension. I do not think the explanation given by the minister is at all satisfactory, and I want to associate myself with the able remarks of the hon. gentlemen who have already taken part in the discussion of this matter, and to say once more that the Indians should be given the old age pension right away. Too many Indians are growing old and will die before we get around to taking care of them by all these measures the minister has mentioned. It will take probably twenty-five years to get the whole Indian population rehabilitated to the point where the aged people will have the chance our white old people now have. What are they to do in the meantime?
Just to show that there is considerable feeling among people who are in a position to be good judges on this matter, I should like to quote two or three statements from briefs which have been submitted by bodies of people whose opinions should be given some respect. The United Church, after having a good deal of experience with the Indians, had this to say in their brief:
The United Church is of the opinion that there is no reason why the Indian people should not participate in any old age pension scheme
Old Age Pensions

set up by the dominion government; and is of the opinion that, in the administration of the scheme, the same conditions should apply as in respect to the old age pension scheme generally, with such modifications as may be necessary to meet the difference in status of the _ Indian people-that is to say, without provincial contributions.
The Roman Catholic church, after having wide experience with the Indians, as everyone knows, had this to say:
It appears to us both fair and desirable that this phase of social legislation-
They were speaking of old age pensions.
-should be extended to the aged Indian who would thus be assured of a definite amount for his declining years of life.
A great many Indian groups presented their case before the committee; in practically every instance those people asked for the old age pension. They asked this simple question: Why should we not have the old age pension? Is there any reason why we should not have it? I have not been able to find that a satisfactory answer has been given to that question. They should have the old age pension; and, as I said before, I want to join with those who have advocated that they be given it.

I wish to say a word or two about section 8 (a) (ii), which is in section 4 of this bill. That section reads: ... if such person
(ii) has resided in Canada for the twenty years immediately preceding the said date or if he has not so resided, has been present in Canada prior to such twenty years for an aggregate period equal to twice the aggregate period of absences from Canada during such twenty years . . .
As I see it, the two parts of that clause do not coordinate at all. The first part deals with the question of twenty-year residence. The second part deals with the period prior to twenty years. If a person has not been here for twenty years, then the twenty-year period has nothing whatever to do with him. For instance, if a person had resided in Canada for fifteen years before reaching the age of seventy, that person would have to wait for another five years before he could get his pension, because the second part of the clause does not work in with the first part at all. Perhaps the minister would explain it.

I think the clause is satisfactory. The law officers believe so, and they think it satisfies what we had in mind. It will admit to pension persons who might have lived most of their lives in Canada but who, because of absence from the country for a number of years in the latter part of their lives, say between the ages of fifty and

seventy, are at present debarred from pension. We all know of many such cases among older people living along the United States boundary, who perhaps go to that country for a few years; and, not having lived here continuously for twenty years find themselves barred. This provides a way to overcome that anomaly if the applicant can show that for every day of absence during the twenty years, he had double the period of residence in this country before the twenty years. In this way we are enabling a great many people who have lived here, worked here and paid taxes here, to get the benefits of this legislation in spite of their absences during that twenty-year period. speechtext: I should like to revert to the subsection dealing with Indians in order to make one comment. I was not on the Indian affairs committee and I shall be very brief. As I understand it, the interim recommendation which the Indian affairs committee made will not be carried out in this bill. The minister stated, if I understood him correctly, the government purpose dealing with the Indians in a comprehensive manner and do not consider it appropriate to deal with them in this bill. That may or may not be right; I am expressing no opinion, but, as matters stand now, people of the Indian race over seventy years of age get a mere fraction of what they would get if they were entitled under this bill. If that is correct it is shocking to me that we should allow this bill to go through without some interim arrangement being made for the Indians. It means that we are dealing with voters and ignoring the non-voters, and we may well have a situation which our own committee has said is a shocking one. I understand, from what the minister said, that the Indians will not be dealt with this year and, it has been suggested, perhaps not for two years. It is not right for people like ourselves to allow that situation to happen.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I wish to say a word on behalf of the Indians because they have very little opportunity to speak for themselves. As the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has said, they do not vote; they have no franchise. The minister has admitted what is, of course, a fact, that the Indians are the wards and the

responsibility of the federal government. The government having admitted that, it seems a downright shame that it is neglecting practically its only direct responsibility in this matter of pensions. The Indian affairs committee approved an interim report in favour of. old age pensions for the Indians, and subsequently delegations of Indians complimented the committee on having rendered the Indians this service. They said it was the finest thing we had ever done. I can imagine, therefore, the disappointment and frustration which will be bound to prevail amongst the Indians in Canada when they find they are not to receive this recognition. I appeal to the minister not to wait until the committee's exhaustive report is made available to the house, because I am only now beginning to appreciate the length of time it is bound to take, and to leave the Indians long in doubt as to their future security in their advancing years is not fair to them.
I would remind the minister that we have now in the Indian affairs branch a complete administrative set-up to make whatever contribution parliament decides to make by way of old age pensions to the Indians. There are representatives on practically every reserve, inspectors for the various provinces and a complete staff of officials, and it seems to me that this would be the ideal moment, in this particular year when Canada is celebrating the eightieth anniversary of confederation, to make this contribution to the welfare of the first citizens of this country. 1 do not believe it could be done simply by striking out the phrase "is not an Indian", because that is repeated elsewhere in the bill. I believe it could be done by introducing a supplement, and I am sure, from the sentiments expressed here, it would be approved rapidly if it provided for the Indians only $20 a month. It would give these unfortunates some sense of security. They are now receiving a pittance of only $5.60 a month to supply themselves with food and clothing and fuel. They have their shelters and they are not subject to tax. We know from experience how much the family allowance has been appreciated by the Indians. It has made a contribution to their educational and general welfare, but the aged Indian is being neglected. They are our oldest citizens. We have only about 130,000 Indians all told, and the number of them seventy years of age and over cannot be very large. Parliament should not be satisfied to prorogue without making some provision for these oldest of our citizens. They are expecting the pension because of the publicity that was given to the interim report of the Indian affairs committee and if

Old Age Pensions
nothing is done for them they will be greatly disappointed.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
So far in this debate I have not had an opportunity of expressing myself one way or the other. Now that we are on section 4, which deals with the amount of the dominion's contribution and defines the persons who are pensionable and the allowable income, I wish to say just a few words.
First, I want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge to this effect, that there is not a corner of this vast dominion which is not concerned in regard to this matter. Articles in the press of the country have stirred the minds of both our young people and our middle-aged as well as our aged citizens. The young people are stirred because they know that old age is inevitable, that some day they will be old, and on account of the lack of an adequate old age pension policy certain sacrifices and demands will be made upon them which are the concern of the state. The middle-aged are of course, concerned because they know that old age is approaching them all too rapidly, and the aged are, of course, concerned because they are in need now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I just want to point out. Mr. Chairman, that what we are doing now is dealing with the principle of the bill. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. gentleman who is speaking for the first time on the bill, and I hope he will not misunderstand me, but I think, as minister piloting the bill, it is my duty to say, that we ought to have a discussion of the specific clauses of the bill, not just general statements which should have been made on the second reading. I suggest that there is no sense in moving the second reading and going into committee of the whole, unless we observe the rules. I would call that to your attention, sir, with great respect.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
If the minister had waited long enough he would have found that I would be discussing the very clause before the committee. I have been thinking about a small group of old age pensioners in my constituency. They are members of the old' age pensioners' association of British Columbia. I know these people. I know the background of their lives, and I am wondering how I am to go back to my constituency and face these people and) tell them that this government is asking them to live on 81 a day. That I believe is pertinent, Mr. Chairman, to the section we are discussing.
Who are these people for whom we are pleading, today? It has been emphasized
again and again in this debate that they are the pioneers who have made Canada what she is today. It has been pointed out in the debate that Canada is one of the richest countries in the world, and one of the best countries in the world to live in, and I agree with all of that. But I still feel that Canada, which made such splendid showing in her war effort, can do more than this bill does for our old age pensioners. As a boy I was always taught to respect old age. I believe that one of the best wavs of estimating character is to watch the attitude of any boy or girl upon the street towards people of advancing age. If we want to honour old age we shall try to be concerned about how our old people are to live when they come to the twilight of their lives.
I believe that we should remove the stigma of charity from our old age pensions. During my forty-two years of life in this dominion I have heard some very hard things said in Canada about expecting one to live to the age of seventy years before one can become eligible for the old age pension. I have heard some hard and bitter things said about the means test. That, too, is involved in this section. I am of the opinion that if a Gallup poll were taken across the Dominion of Canada today there would be an overwhelming expression of opinion that the means test should be abolished forthwith.
One thing, of course, is interesting in this debate on aid age pensions, and that is that it cuts across all party lines. Everyone is agreed that we should do all that is humanly possible for our aged citizens, especially when we look at the advanced cost of living. It has been rising from day to day, and I personally cannot see much prospect of improvement in this regard. Statisticians may produce their charts to show just how much such and such a plan would cost the country, but I should like to point out to the committee tonight that the amount for which we are asking for our old age pensioners is nothing comparable with the cost of battleships which we built during the war years and sank on all oceans of the world. I have not heard it said in the debate so far what these old age pensioners are supposed to do with this money. Suppose we give them S50 a month at the age of sixty-five, as we are asking the government to do. Will they put it in a stocking? Will they hoard the money? I do not think so. This money will be spent in the stores of our country. It will be another method of distributing purchasing power. It will act like a shot in the arm to business. The country and the government will get the bulk of this money back again in taxes either directly or indirectly, because every time an old age pensioner walks
Old Age Pensions

into a grocery store to buy some article of food he will be paying in directly some of the taxes which will bring the money back to the government.
In a debate on this subject which took place on April 10, 1946, the then minister of national health and welfare, present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), placed on Hansard, at page 752, a chart of estimates of the cost of old age pensions for the years 1948, 1951, 1961 and 1971. He was striving to show that the government's proposals to the provinces constituted a burden which could be carried by the Canadian economy. He admitted on page 753 of Hansard that we could have pensions of the size advocated, namely, $50 at the age of sixty-five, but that the increased cost would have to come from one of three sources, either taxes or borrowing or printed money.
It is abundantly clear that the government's hesitation today arises out of the question, where is the money to come from? Several hon. members tonight have been generous enough to hand bouquets to the minister, and I am glad to say that he has appreciated them with a smile. I want to say that I feel rather sorry for him. Perhaps he might not enjoy my pity, but I think-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I appreciate the hon. member's interest.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I think he has just been handed a very difiiicult portfolio as Minister of National Health and Welfare. He is handling it intelligently, and with all due regard to his great task I think he is doing a good job. But when this bill came before the house I should have liked to see him go out to the country with a bold measure which would have given an adequate pension for our aged citizens, and I believe the country would have supported him in that move.
So far as I have read the articles in the press, there has been very little said. The press generally is waiting to see what parliament will do, and they will not have to wait very long.
There is a phrase in this section which deals with allowable income. It is my opinion that very few of our aged citizens will be blessed by receiving very much of this allowable income. Many of them have reached the stage where they are no longer of value on the labour market. Even if they were, work is not obtainable by them. I know that during 1941, under the exigencies of war, there was work for almost everybody. It was not a question of age or of youth. Even in my own constituency of Kootenay East in

1941 both old and young had no difficulty whatever in obtaining work of one kind or another, but the picture is entirely changed today. Women of the age of sixty are being let out of their jobs, and men of the age of sixty-five are being let out by government departments. I am concerned about how these people are to live between the ages of sixty-five and seventy when, under this bill, they become eligible for old age pension. Something should be done for these people and it is a government responsibility to see that those who, through no fault of their own, have not been able to accumulate anything for their aged years shall not be allowed slowly to starve to death as many of them are undoubtedly doing.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to say one word regarding our Indian population, since others have been doing the same. I do not know how many hon. members have ever had the privilege of living on Indian reserves. I suppose most hon. members have Indian tribes fairly adjacent to them in their constituencies, but I have lived on Indian reserves in British Columbia for over twelve years, and I know something about how these people live. If there is one thing that is needed, and one place in which the minister can bring some glory to himself-not that he is looking for that kind of thing-a place in which he can really do a first-rate job for the Dominion of Canada, it is to see that the old age pension is made payable to the Indians of our dominion just as soon as possible. They need it, if anybody does; and, as was hinted by the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario, if these people had votes, then they would be considered far more than they are considered today. But they have not the right to vote. They do pay taxes. They pay indirect taxes as well as other people, and because of that they have a right. The very fact that these are the original inhabitants of this country gives them rights, and this discrimination should be done away with just as speedily as possible. Give the old age pension to the Indian population as well as to the white population.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I wish to say one or two words. I know the committee will generously allow me these few words. I appreciate what the hon. gentleman has just said. All the criticisms that have been heaped on me I expected and I accept them, because in a measure of this kind, where some think you are not doing enough and others think you are doing too much, naturally one is placed in a difficult position; but I want to say to the hon. gentleman that I have at least this to console me. Through this bill I have been

Old Age Pensions
somewhat responsible for bringing to 275,000 people in this country something in the way of improved living conditions. It may not be the kind of relief that all hon. members think we should have brought. But by this bill I am being the instrument-and that is the only way I will put it-of bringing to 60,000 people for the first time the opportunity of receiving the old age pension. I say that it might not be what all hon. members think it should be but in the light of all obligations, and in the light of great objectives which we seek as a government, I relish the fact that at least I have been able to help to do that much.

speechtext: From the trend of the discussion it would appear that the Indians are left on their own as they become old. I think it is only fair to the Indians, the members of the house and to the people of Canada generally that we should let it be known that to a greater extent the older Indians are given care and attention. I might cite one instance which is well known to many members of the house who were on the commission last fall. I refer to the case of an elderly Indian couple of Shubenacadie, Nova Scotia, who were .moved to a new home, a very comfortable place, which had been built for them. It consisted of two large rooms, one used as a livingroom and bedroom, and the other used as kitchen and diningroom. The government had supplied them with the essentials such as food and also, I believe, with certain animals such as a pig-

Of course, when the opposition get through talking, probably we shall be able to accomplish a few things that are vitally needed by the Indian population. So far as I can see, there are many things to be accomplished on their behalf, and everyone who has any knowledge of the matter knows that. On the other hand, the Indians themselves, with the help of the government, have made great strides in the last few years, and that is something for which we should be grateful.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I was surprised to see the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) coming to the help of the minister and whitewashing the treatment of the Indians in this country in what I thought was really a feeble way. As a matter of fact, all that talk of that kind does is to becloud the issue. The fact that there is an odd Indian who is reasonably well looked after has nothing to do with the general situation that the Indians are not receiving adequate help in their old1 age. The actual fact, which the hon. member knows as well as I do, is that the Indians receive the equivalent in kind-rice, flour, lard, salt, tea and so forth -of about $5 to $6 a month, depending on the locality in which they live. That is what they receive as old age benefits, and it is totally inadequate as nearly everyone in the house will admit. I do not think we should becloud the issue. We should look at the matter honestly and admit that we have not treated these people properly.
I am not putting the blame on this government but on all governments that have been in office in this country. I do not think there should be anything along the line of politics in this matter. There certainly is not as far as I am concerned, and at the present time we should look at the matter from the point of view of what is necessary for these old Indians. The minister, I am sorry to say, in replying to the hon. member for Peterborough West, also misled or attempted to mislead the committee-

Unintentionally, I should have said. The Indians who volunteered or were conscripted., as some were, and served in 
the armed forces of the country during the war, by virtue of their service have the right to vote, but have no right to draw old age pension when they reach the age, because they are still Indians under the act and the statement that the minister made that they may become enfranchised is completely begging the question. It has nothing to do with the situation, which is this. A man who either volunteered or was conscripted for service and fought for the country is denied the right to old age pension because he is an Indian under the act, whereas thousands of people who had no service as far as this country is concerned and many of whom were conscientious objectors and refused to fight, are eligible for the pension. That in itself is one of the inconsistencies which cannot be defended. It is a complete inconsistency that that situation could exist.
Before I sit down I should like to refer to a quotation I gave from "King Lear", while I was speaking half an hour or so ago. When I quoted this tag the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, who is a great student of Shakespeare, immediately sent for a copy; and after I had resumed my seat he called me over and said, "You know, I think you have added a few lines to Shakespeare. I do not think you can possibly find those lines in 'King Lear,' " He said, "Here is the book", and he challenged me to find them. I have now found the lines, and they run in this way:
But mice and rats and such small deer Have been Tom's food for seven long year.
The quotation goes on-and I am sure there are many Indians who would subscribe to this part of it also, as far as the white people of this country are concerned-and ends in this way:
Peace, Smulkin; peace, thou fiend.

speechtext:
I wish to ask the minister a question on this section; but, before doing so, I wish to state that I have listened patiently to a great many speeches and some very good arguments on this section and on the Old Age Pensions Act. Despite what the minister stated with regard to some people agreeing that this was too much, I have not heard that argument advanced in this house. I have not heard an hon. member state that $30 a month was an adequate pension. I have heard a good many arguments advanced to the effect that it was probably the largest amount we could pay at the present time, having regard to our obligations with respect to other social security measures. That argument may have some validity, but certainly there is no validity to any argument which contends that this is an adequate pension. We in this group have stated that we believe that $50 a month would be an adequate pension, having regard to our ability to produce
Old Age Pensions

in this country. I wish to state why we think that. If hon. members will cast their minds back to when the war started in 1939, they will remember that our national income in Canada was approximately three and a quarter billion to three and a half billion dollars. Today that national income is something over nine billion dollars.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Eleven billion dollars.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Well, it is at least two and a half times what it was before the recent war started. If we go back and look at the income earned by the farmers of this country, we shall find that in the six years prior to this war their average earned income was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $700. We shall find the same thing if we go back to the earnings of industrial workers. Today we find those incomes are approximately two and a half times what they were during the 1930's. If $20 a month was an adequate pension in the 1930's-and I do not think it was, but it was the pension which we were paying out of our total production in this country at that time -then I say that today, with production two and a half times as large as it was at that time, a fair pension to the old people of this country would be two and a half times what they were getting in the 1930's, or $50 a month. I would ask the minister if that is not a fair argument. Last year we exported from this country some $600,000,000 worth more goods than we brought back in. In other words, we sent out goods and services to that extent to help Europe and to build up reserves of pounds, francs and currencies in those other countries, which we did not use for the purpose of bringing back goods to this country, because in many cases those goods were not being produced in those countries. But I say that if our national income today is two and a half times what it was in the thirties, and if we can afford to export $600 million worth of goods more than we import, then we should be able to give our old age pensioners in this country better than $30 a month. I think that is a sound argument. I agree that we cannot feed our old age pensioners or clothe them with locomotives and materials of that kind, but we can feed and clothe them with goods we can bring back in return for those exports. I say that when we are capable of producing all these goods and services we should be prepared to share them with the old people of this country.

I want to reply to what the hon. gentleman has said, because I think his question is important and I should like to bring this matter to a finality. My hon. friend

keeps speaking of a pension of $30. Technically that is correct under this bill, but one should bear in mind what flows from the passage of this bill. It means that in British Columbia, for instance, without the province spending one further cent per pensioner, the pension rate can be raised to $38.75. It means that in Alberta the rate can be $33.75, without the province spending an extra cent per pensioner. It means that in Saskatchewan the rate can be $33.75 without the province spending one cent more per pensioner. In Ontario, up to the day before the bill was introduced, it meant a pension of $31.75, but that province has now increased its pension to $40 as a result of this bill. One must bear those things in mind.

why one province cannot do as much as another province. That is the last type of argument the minister should be using if he wants to secure cooperation; and I must say I have been disappointed in the minister in that respect.	.

I made a suggestion to the minister in regard to the wives of pensioners who were not eligible for pension in their own right. I suggested that he take the matter under consideration and perhaps be prepared to do something for this fairly large number of our citizens. Let us take the case of a pensioner seventy years of age or over. Very likely his wife will be somewhere between sixty and sixty-five, or at least under seventy. She will not be eligible for the pension until she is seventy years of age. If the total income of that man and wife, who have made their contribution as citizens to the welfare of Canada, is $30 a month, or $360 a year-it may be more in some of the provinces mentioned a moment ago by the minister, though even in British Columbia, which pays the highest pension next to Ontario, it would be only $35 a month, or $420 a year-does the minister suggest to this committee that any family can live on $360 or $420 a year? As the hon. member for Melfort' has said, the minister studiously avoided mentioning the maritime provinces. I think I read it the other day, but may I read again a short paragraph from the proposals made by the dominion government in 1945, specifically on the question of old age pensions? This is at page 37:
There are considerable variations between the provinces in respect of the number of persons obtaining pensions and the average amount of pension paid. Thus, in one province 28 per cent of all persons aged seventy and over were receiving old age pensions in 1945, and in another province 57 per cent. Likewise, the amount of average monthly pension varies from $18.63 per month in one province to $29.41 (including pro-incial supplement) in another.
Granted that this has been increased in the provinces where supplements are paid, it has not been increased in those provinces where no provincial supplement is paid. This is what I want the minister and the committee to listen to and understand:
Generally speaking, the need for pensions is, as might be expected, greatest in those provinces which are least able to finance such payments out of local revenues.
It is those provinces which are least able to pay the supplement from their local revenues, and which are not paying supplemental pensions, that the minister neglects to mention when he gives the pensions being paid. And it must be remembered that there is nothing in this bill which provides
that there shall be a pension of $30 a month. Let me read the section, so that I will not leave anything out:
Pursuant to an agreement made with a province under section three of this act, the government of Canada will contribute in respect of each person in receipt of pension from such province an amount not to exceed seventy-five per centum of thirty dollars monthly or of the amount paid by such province monthly, whichever is the lesser, for pension to each such person . . .
This clearly provides that in some provinces the pension will probably not be $30 a month, because those provinces will not be able to pay that amount from their local revenues.

The minister is concerned solely with dominion matters. I think there has been altogether too much talk about what the provinces are going to do, particularly on the part of the minister. He made that his main theme when he was not talking about political things in the address he gave in introducing the bill. In doing that, I think he made a tremendous mistake, if I may suggest such a thing to one of his experience. The bland and cool assumption has been made that the provinces will continue something which they have been doing because the dominion has refused to live up to its responsibilties, and when I say the dominion, I mean the dominion government. But I am quite sure that some of the supplementary payments which were made by the provinces to eke out the meagre dominion grant were made on a temporary basis. They were made in the hope that the dominion would at some time live up to its responsibilities. Of course that hope was based largely on the expectation that there would be a dominion-provincial agreement. That has not happened, and we find ourselves in our present predicament. I think the minister was presumptuous in his speech to suggest that the provinces should pay a certain amount, He has done it again tonight. He

said that British Columbia would pay $38.65, or whatever it is, and that Saskatchewan would pay $33.75. The minister has no guarantee that the provinces will continue to make those payments.

I have been very patient all through this debate, not having said a word since April 24 on old age pensions. I think that is showing pretty good patience for this house when it is realized that some bon. members have been up and down at least half a dozen times. I wish to do like one or two others have done. I want to pay a personal compliment to the minister, because every time some hon. member suggests that something should be done for the Indians the minister expresses an expansive sympathy for the plight of the Indians. I think that is a commendable thing when the minister or anybody else indicates that he has such great sympathy, and his sympathy embraced the whole house. He said that every member of the house would agree with him in that sympathy. That includes the members on his own side. But unfortunately, when a practical concrete thing is suggested to make use of some of that sympathy then like Pharaoh's heart of old his heart hardens and the house is left trying to make bricks without straw. That is about what has been happening in the debate so far.
Another source of satisfaction to me tonight is that something has occurred during this debate that I have never before seen occur to such an extent. When we were discussing the orders in council under the omnibus bill in April and were dealing with sections referring to old age pensions I introduced the idea that
when the breadwinner of a family unit in this country becomes of pensionable age and qualifies for pension under the means test, his dependent spouse should also receive the pension. That idea has been echoed now by several members on the other side of the house and by quite a few members in all parts of the house, and I take great satisfaction from that because, since I have been a member of this house, I had never heard anyone make that suggestion until I introduced it on that day.

If the minister really believed that, let me draw his attention to subparagraph (i) of paragraph (c) of the section under discussion at the present time. We find that the pension and the outside income that a pensioner is allowed to have must not amount to more than $50 a month. If he gets more than that his pension is reduced. . . . married to and living with a sighted spouse.
In that case their pension and outside income altogether may be $1,080 a year, indicating that in those circumstances the dependent spouse is not worth quite as much or will not cost quite as much to keep as an individual without sight, but if he is married to a blind spouse, it is $120 more, which is more like a living allowance. I hope that the people who come under subparagraph (ii) do not get tempted, if they are not too moral, to take their spouses' eyes out and send them out with a tin-cup to beg enough to make up the $120. There is that difference between the two. Certainly there does not seem to be any good reason why those under (ii) should not be allowed as much pension and outside income as those under (iii). I am not asking that (iii) be reduced to the amount in (ii) in these paragraphs, but that (ii) be increased in conformity with (iii).

The question I wish to ask is the one I asked when I spoke on the second reading of the bill. Various other hon. members raised it at that time, and various hon. members have raised it tonight. My question is why the principle of the war veterans allowance has not been applied in this bill, so that a pension may be paid to both the wife and the husband, even though the age of the wife may be below seventy. After all, I believe the husband is supposed to be responsible for his wife. Therefore, when he reaches the age of seventy and receives $360 a year, if his wife is less than seventy the couple have to live on $360 a year, which means that they are living on $180 each, which is only fifty cents a day. I should like the minister to answer the question as to whether or not the government has given any consideration to applying the principle of the war veterans allowance to this measure.

and I am quite sure everybody in the house was perfectly honest about it-because we all realized that it was impossible to live on the old indemnity in view of the increase in taxation and the cost of living. My only point in mentioning that is that, if we could not live on our indemnity, how can we expect thousands of our old citizens to live on $1 a day? I say they cannot live on that. And if they cannot, what are they to do? That is what I want to be told. How are they to live on $1 a day? It certainly is out of all reason to expect them to do so in this day and age. If there were any prospect that the amount would be increased next year, the situation might be different. But apparently this is to be more or less permanent. I understood the minister to say a few minutes ago that the pensioners cannot live on that amount, and they are not supposed to live on it. WThat are they to do, then? $2,000 for the members of this house in consideration of the fact that we were intending to bring down a decent rate of pensions, not only for the old age pensioners, but for all people who are physically incapacitated.
There is one other point I should like to mention in regard to pensions of $50 a month. The question which is being continually raised is whether we can afford it. As I said on second reading, in my opinion we cannot afford not to pay oldi age pensions at a decent rate; we must do it, not merely for the purpose of providing old age pensioners with a decent standard of living, but for the purpose of helping to make our present system function. As the Minister of Finance has warned, the greatest danger we in this country face in the near future is lack of effective demand. One of the best ways of helping to build up effective demand in this country is to pay old age pensioners $50 a month. That is quite in order, and bears directly on this section of the bill. What is one of the best ways of helping to maintain effective demand in this country against the production of the country? We in this group, and I think all members on this side of the house, feel that one of the best ways of doing that is by providing decent social services; and old age pensions should probably have priority over all such social services unless it is decent pension to all those people who are physically incapacitated. I should like to ask the minister whether or not the government have given consideration to that question. I should imagine they have, because it is a matter which was raised iby the Minister of Finance and by the governor of the Bank of Canada, when they said the great danger we in this country are facing in the very near future is the lack of effective demand. Iif we cannot maintain effective demand against the production of the country, then our national income will fall. And if our national income falls, we shall find it that much harder to finance old age pensions of even $30 a month.

I think it is important that we should have some such reciprocal arrangement at this time. A number of our people have married Australians or New Zealanders, or have brought home English brides, and there is no doubt that, as they become older, a considerable number of our people will wish to go to other parts of the commonwealth, perhaps to stay with relatives. This matter should be given consideration, and I suppose that will be done, in view of the minister's statement. I should have liked to see the minister able to make some definite statement as to how far these negotiations have progressed; but, in view of the fact that the matter is still under discussion, I suppose it would be impossible for him to go any farther than he has done tonight in this respect.
There has been a good deal of discussion as to the adequacy of the $30 a month mentioned in this section. I notice order No. 10 on the order paper, which reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to present a measure to provide pensions or other superannuation benefits for senior appointees of the Department of External Affairs serving outside Canada and the wives, widows and dependants thereof.
I wonder if the government will consider $30 a month sufficient for those people, because apparently they consider $30 a month sufficient for our old people. In view of what we have voted for ourselves; in view of our generous treatment of returned men; in view of our very generous treatment of judges; in view of our very generous treatment of various [The Chairman.]
other civil servants in this country, it seems to me that we certainly should be prepared at this time to be a little more generous with our old people. I believe I have shown that out of the total national income of this country, which has increased to approximately three times what it was in the thirties, a fair share to our old people would be $50 a month. It seems to me that should be the minimum we can afford out of our production at this time. It is not asking too much that our senior citizens share with the rest of us on a fair basis. We have all increased our incomes in the last five or six years. There is not a member in this house whose income today is not two or three times what it was in the thirties.
